History:
- Presenting complaint: 2–3 days of chest tightness, wheeze, cough and exertional shortness of breath.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began while running 2–3 days ago (previously tolerated running); now symptomatic with brisk walking as well. Symptoms persistent since onset and described as a small exacerbation.
- Triggers/timing/associated symptoms: Symptoms provoked by exercise; reports wheeze and coughing. No sputum production. Has seasonal hay fever. No fever or systemic viral symptoms documented.
- Past episodes: Last significant asthma attack ~3–4 years ago. Last asthma review ~2 years ago.

Past Medical History:
- Known asthma.
- Hay fever (allergic rhinitis).
- Possible eczema (uses topical hydrocortisone and Cetraben for skin; patient uncertain).
- Family history: brother with asthma, sister with eczema.
- Allergies: No medication allergies reported.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (blue reliever) — dose/route/frequency not documented; used as needed and reportedly "not helping."
  - Inhaled steroid preventer (Clenil/beclomethasone) — used twice daily (exact dose/puff count not documented).
  - Topical hydrocortisone — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Cetraben (emollient) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- No prior oral steroid courses recalled. No previous hospital admissions for asthma recorded.
- Smoking status: Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
- Reported/observed findings from history:
  - Wheeze (patient-reported).
  - Cough (patient-reported).
  - Shortness of breath, worse on exertion.
  - No sputum production reported.
- Objective exam/vitals: Not recorded. Doctor planned chest examination and peak flow measurement at GP face-to-face review.

Impression:
- Most likely: Acute asthma exacerbation (exercise-provoked) — patient with known asthma presenting with new/worsening wheeze, cough and exertional dyspnea over 2–3 days and increased reliever use.
- Other plausible diagnoses consistent with transcript:
  - Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) — onset during running and provoked by exertion; atopic history (hay fever) supports risk.
  - Viral respiratory infection triggering asthma exacerbation — short duration cough/wheeze could reflect viral trigger.
- (DDx and transcript: consistent; no conflict noted.)

Management Plan:
- Immediate advice given:
  - Continue/use salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed; advised maximum frequency while awaiting review — up to every 2–4 hours (use frequently indicates severe control issue; seek urgent care if worsening).
  - Increase inhaled steroid (brown Clenil) while awaiting GP: advised increase to 4 puffs twice daily (doctor instruction to increase preventer dose).
- Safety advice:
  - If breathing significantly worsens or fails to improve, present to A&E without waiting for GP appointment.
- Pending/possible treatments at face-to-face GP visit:
  - Chest examination and peak flow measurement.
  - Consider oral steroids and/or antibiotics depending on assessment and findings.
- Follow-up:
  - Face-to-face GP appointment recommended within a few days for assessment and objective testing.

Patient Summary:
- Young adult with known asthma developed wheeze, cough and exertional shortness of breath over the past 2–3 days beginning during a run. Salbutamol is being used with limited benefit; preventer inhaler is in use but may be suboptimally dosed. Plan is interim increase in inhaled steroid and reliever use as advised, with expedited GP review and instruction to go to A&E if symptoms worsen.

Key Takeaways:
- Increase brown inhaler (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily while waiting for GP review.
- Use blue reliever (salbutamol) as needed (up to every 2–4 hours); seek immediate emergency care if breathing deteriorates.
- Attend face-to-face GP appointment for chest exam and peak flow; steroids/antibiotics may be started if indicated.

Next Steps:
- Book and attend GP face-to-face review within next few days.
- At GP visit: perform chest examination and repeat peak flow measurement (compare to reported baseline ~380 L/min).
- If clinical assessment indicates, start oral corticosteroids and/or antibiotics per GP judgment.
- Medication reconciliation and confirmation of inhaler technique/doses at review.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: current vital signs (heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature), current measured peak flow, smoking status, exact current puff dose/frequency for inhalers, inhaler technique review, objective chest exam findings, any recent travel/PE risk factors.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx is consistent with transcript.
- Transcript quality: Mostly clear; occasional brief unclear phrases about medication names/doses (patient and clinician statements about exact preventer puff count were not fully confirmed).
